newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: EU appeals at WTO over ruling on bananas.
newsitem.headline: EU appeals at WTO over ruling on bananas.

text.p: The European Union lodged an appeal with the World Trade Organisation (WTO) on Wednesday against a panel finding which said its banana import policies violated WTO open trading rules.
The appeal, which had been widely expected, emerged just 24 hours before Brussels would have had to explain to the WTO's Dispute Settlement Body (DSB) how it would implement the finding.

The three-man panel, in a ruling that dismayed banana-producing states in the Caribbean and delighted their Latin American competitors, said on April 29 that a U.S. complaint against the EU "banana regime" was well-founded.

The United States argued the intricate web of EU regulations favouring banana imports from former European colonies, which rely on sales of the fruit for most of their foreign revenues, discriminated against U.S.-based marketing companies.

The case against the EU was strongly supported by major Latin American banana producers, including Ecuador, Honduras, Mexico and Guatemala, which asserted that the regime amounted to an unfair barrier against their exports.
Under WTO rules, the EU now has 10 days to provide a detailed reasoning for its appeal, which can only be based on issues of law and legal interpretations not on the substance of the panel's report.

A three-member appeals board will have up to three months from Tuesday to produce its report -- but diplomats said this could be extended because of the complicated nature of the case and the vast documentation involved.

Once the board makes its report and it is adopted by the DSB, the EU -- if its case is rejected -- would have a month to tell the DSD how it plans to bring the banana import regulations into line with the panel findings.

If it declines, the DSB -- on which all members of the 131-state WTO sit -- can authorise the United States and the other complainants to take trade measures against the EU to the value of the trade they say they have lost.

Caribbean banana producers have bitterly criticised the United States for bringing the case, which they say is aimed at ensuring profits for big U.S. companies like Chiquita Brands and Dole and ignores their dependence on the fruit.

They have said that if the EU is compelled to implement the ruling, their economies could be devastated and warned that this could lead to an increase in illegal trade in narcotics -- which would rebound on the United States.

The United States has argued its stance is aimed at discrimination by the EU in favour of its own banana-marketing companies and not at limiting exports from the Caribbean and other former European colonies in Africa and the Pacific.
